items.stem: X₁,…,Xₙ are iid with density f(x;θ) = θx^(θ−1) on 0 < x < 1, θ > 0. The MLE of θ is:
items.explanation: ℓ(θ) = n log θ + (θ−1)Σ log xᵢ. Then dℓ/dθ = n/θ + Σ log xᵢ = 0, so θ̂ = −n/Σ log xᵢ. The minus sign is required and is what makes θ̂ positive, since every log xᵢ < 0 on (0,1). Option B has the wrong sign and would return a negative estimate.

items.stem: A geometric sample (number of trials to the first success, support 1,2,3,…) of size n = 6 has Σxᵢ = 24. Give the MLE of p and the MLE of the expected number of trials.
options: p̂ = 0.25 and the MLE of E[X] is 0.75
p̂ = 0.25 and the MLE of E[X] is 4
p̂ = 0.20 and the MLE of E[X] is 5
p̂ = 4 and the MLE of E[X] is 0.25
items.explanation: P(X=x) = (1−p)^(x−1) p, so ℓ(p) = n log p + (Σxᵢ − n) log(1−p). Setting the derivative to zero gives p̂ = n/Σxᵢ = 6/24 = 0.25. E[X] = 1/p, so by invariance its MLE is 1/0.25 = 4, which is x̄.
items.check: p̂ and 1/p̂ are both plausible-looking answers. Confirm which the question asked for.

items.stem: X₁,…,Xₙ are iid U(0,θ) and θ̂ = x₍ₙ₎ is the MLE.
items.explanation: A is true — the derivative never vanishes, so the usual method does not locate the maximum. B is true: x₍ₙ₎ ≤ θ always, and E[θ̂] = nθ/(n+1) < θ. C is false — x₍ₙ₎ is the complete sufficient statistic and the MLE is a function of it. D is true: scaling by (n+1)/n removes the bias.
statements: The score equation dℓ/dθ = 0 has no solution for this model.
θ̂ is not a function of the sufficient statistic.

A.why: dℓ/dθ = −n/θ < 0 wherever L > 0. It is never zero.

B.why: The sample maximum cannot exceed θ, and equals it with probability 0.

C.why: x₍ₙ₎ IS the sufficient statistic here, so the MLE is trivially a function of it.

D.why: E[x₍ₙ₎] = nθ/(n+1), so multiplying by (n+1)/n gives θ exactly.

items.stem: A sample of n = 16 from N(μ, σ²) with both unknown gives Σxᵢ = 80 and Σ(xᵢ − x̄)² = 60. Give the MLE of σ², the unbiased estimator s², and say which is larger.
items.explanation: The MLE divides by n: σ̂² = 60/16 = 3.75. The unbiased estimator divides by n−1: s² = 60/15 = 4. Since n−1 < n, s² is always the larger of the two, and the MLE is biased low by a factor (n−1)/n = 15/16.
items.check: Two numbers and a comparison were asked for. The n versus n−1 choice is the whole question — write which denominator you used.

items.stem: If θ̂ is the MLE of θ and the parameter of interest is ψ = e^(−2θ), then the MLE of ψ is:
options: It cannot be obtained without a fresh derivation
items.explanation: Invariance: the MLE of any function g(θ) is g(θ̂), so ψ̂ = e^(−2θ̂) directly. Option B is the derivative, not the estimator. Option C confuses the MLE with an expectation — and note e^(−2θ̂) is generally a biased estimator of e^(−2θ), which is consistent with the MLE not being unbiased.

items.stem: Consider the likelihood function L(θ) for a fixed observed sample.
items.explanation: A is false — L is a function of θ but is not a probability distribution over θ and need not integrate to 1. B is true. C is false: the maximiser is unchanged by taking logs, which is precisely why we do it. D is true, by the factorisation theorem.
statements: L(θ) is a probability density function of θ and integrates to 1 over the parameter space.
L(θ) is computed from the data actually observed, held fixed.
Maximising log L(θ) can give a different maximiser from maximising L(θ).
L(θ) depends on the data only through a sufficient statistic, when one exists.

A.why: It is not a distribution for θ. Treating it as one is the single commonest misconception in the topic.

B.why: That is the definition — the data are fixed and θ varies.

C.why: log is strictly increasing, so the maximiser is identical.

D.why: L(θ) = g(T(x);θ)·h(x), and h does not involve θ.

items.stem: X₁,…,Xₙ are iid Exponential(λ). Fisher information for a single observation is I(λ) = 1/λ². For n = 25 and λ̂ = 0.4, the approximate standard error of λ̂ from the asymptotic distribution is:
items.explanation: Asymptotically λ̂ ~ N(λ, 1/(nI(λ))). Here 1/(nI(λ)) = λ²/n, so the SE is λ/√n, estimated as λ̂/√n = 0.4/5 = 0.08.
items.check: √n = 5, not 25. Taking the root of n is the step most often dropped here.

items.stem: Which of the following is NOT guaranteed for a maximum likelihood estimator, even under the usual regularity conditions?
items.explanation: Consistency, asymptotic normality and invariance all hold. Unbiasedness does not: the normal variance MLE is biased low and the exponential rate MLE is biased high, at every finite n. Regularity conditions buy asymptotic behaviour, not finite-sample unbiasedness.

items.stem: A sample of size n = 3 from U(0,θ) gives observations 1.2, 3.8 and 2.5. The MLE of θ, the MLE of θ², and E[θ̂] are:
items.explanation: θ̂ = x₍ₙ₎ = 3.8, the sample maximum. By invariance the MLE of θ² is 3.8² = 14.44. And E[x₍ₙ₎] = nθ/(n+1) = 3θ/4, which understates θ — the sample maximum can never exceed it.
items.check: Three quantities asked, and the third is in terms of θ, not a number. Answering only θ̂ = 3.8 is the wrong-quantity error in its purest form.

items.stem: A question gives a density whose support is 0 < x < θ. Arrange the steps you should take, in order.
items.explanation: Check the support first — that single check decides the whole method. Seeing it depends on θ, abandon the derivative, locate the maximum on the boundary at x₍ₙ₎, and only then answer any follow-up about bias or a function of θ. Starting with the derivative wastes the time the check would have saved.
items: A. Identify the maximum at the boundary θ̂ = x₍ₙ₎
B. Check whether the support depends on θ
C. Address any follow-up on bias or on a function of θ
D. Conclude the score equation does not apply

items.stem: The maximum likelihood estimate of θ is the value that:
options: equates the sample mean to the population mean
makes the estimator unbiased for θ
maximises the likelihood of the observed sample
items.explanation: The MLE is defined by maximisation of L(θ) at the observed data, nothing else. Unbiasedness is not required and frequently fails; minimum MSE is a different criterion altogether; and equating moments is the method of moments.

items.stem: X₁,…,X₈ are iid Poisson(λ) with Σxᵢ = 24. Give the MLE of λ and the MLE of P(X = 0) = e^(−λ).
items.explanation: λ̂ = x̄ = 24/8 = 3. By invariance, the MLE of any function g(λ) is g(λ̂), so the MLE of e^(−λ) is e^(−3) = 0.0498. Option B is the UMVUE of e^(−λ), a different estimator answering a different question — it is unbiased, while the MLE is not.
items.check: Invariance means you substitute, you do not re-derive. If the question had asked for the UMVUE the answer would be ((n−1)/n)^T instead.

items.stem: Consider maximum likelihood estimation in general.
items.explanation: A is true — this is invariance, and it holds for any function. B is false: MLEs are frequently biased, σ̂² for the normal being the standard case. C is true: under regularity the MLE is consistent and asymptotically normal with variance 1/(nI(θ)). D is true — for U(0,θ) the likelihood is maximised at the boundary x₍ₙ₎, where the derivative is never zero.
statements: If θ̂ is the MLE of θ, then g(θ̂) is the MLE of g(θ).
Under regularity the MLE is asymptotically efficient.
The MLE need not be found by setting a derivative to zero.

A.why: The invariance property, valid for any function g, one-to-one or not.

C.why: √n(θ̂−θ) → N(0, 1/I(θ)), so it attains the bound in the limit.

D.why: A boundary maximum, as for U(0,θ), is found by inspecting the likelihood, not differentiating it.

items.stem: X₁,…,X₁₀ are iid Bernoulli(p) with Σxᵢ = 3. Give the MLE of p and the MLE of the odds p/(1−p).
items.explanation: p̂ = x̄ = 3/10 = 0.3. By invariance the MLE of p/(1−p) is p̂/(1−p̂) = 0.3/0.7 = 3/7 ≈ 0.4286. Option D inverts the ratio, giving the odds against rather than the odds for.
items.check: With p̂ below 0.5 the odds must come out below 1. An answer above 1 has the ratio upside down.

items.stem: For X₁,…,Xₙ iid U(0,θ), why is the MLE found without differentiating?
options: The likelihood is not a function of θ
The likelihood is θ^(−n) on θ ≥ x₍ₙ₎ and 0 below it, so it is maximised at the left endpoint of its support
The derivative of the log-likelihood has no solution anywhere
items.explanation: L(θ) = θ^(−n)·I(θ ≥ x₍ₙ₎) is strictly decreasing wherever it is positive, so the maximum sits at the smallest admissible θ, namely x₍ₙ₎. The derivative is −nθ^(−n−1), never zero, which is why setting it to zero finds nothing: the maximum is at a boundary, not at a stationary point.

items.stem: X₁,…,X₂₀ are iid N(μ, σ²) with both unknown. The sample gives Σxᵢ = 60 and Σ(xᵢ − x̄)² = 76. Give the MLE of σ² and the unbiased estimator s², and say which is larger.
options: σ̂² = 4.0 and s² = 3.8, so σ̂² is larger
σ̂² = 3.8 and s² = 4.0, so s² is larger
items.explanation: The MLE divides by n: σ̂² = 76/20 = 3.8. The unbiased estimator divides by n−1: s² = 76/19 = 4.0. Since n−1 < n the unbiased version is always the larger of the two, and the gap closes as n grows — which is the MLE's bias, E[σ̂²] = (n−1)σ²/n, written as a number.
items.check: s² > σ̂² always, for any sample. If your two numbers come out the other way round, the divisors have been swapped.

items.stem: X₁,…,Xₙ are iid Exponential with mean θ.
items.explanation: A is true — the likelihood equation gives θ̂ = x̄. B is true, and here the MLE happens to be unbiased, since E[X̄] = θ. C is false: the MLE of the RATE λ = 1/θ is 1/x̄ by invariance, and that one IS biased, with E[1/X̄] = nλ/(n−1). D is true: Var(X̄) = θ²/n, which equals the Cramér–Rao bound for θ.
statements: The MLE of θ is x̄.
The MLE of θ is unbiased.
The MLE of the rate λ = 1/θ is also unbiased.
The MLE of θ attains the Cramér–Rao bound.

A.why: ℓ = −n log θ − Σx/θ, and setting ℓ′ = 0 gives θ̂ = x̄.

B.why: E[X̄] = θ exactly, at every n.

C.why: Invariance preserves the MLE, not unbiasedness: E[n/ΣX] = nλ/(n−1) > λ.

D.why: I(θ) = 1/θ², so the floor is θ²/n = Var(X̄). Attained.

items.stem: A sample of size n = 5 from U(0,θ) gives the observations 2.4, 0.9, 3.7, 1.1 and 3.2. Give the MLE of θ.
items.explanation: The MLE for U(0,θ) is the sample maximum, so θ̂ = 3.7. Option A is x̄ = 11.3/5 = 2.26, option C is the moment estimator 2x̄ = 4.52, and option D is half the maximum. Note any answer below 3.7 is impossible, since a 3.7 was observed.
items.check: Compare any candidate against the largest observation. Below it, the likelihood is exactly zero.

items.stem: Which is NOT a general property of maximum likelihood estimators?
items.explanation: Invariance holds always; consistency and asymptotic normality hold under the usual regularity conditions. Unbiasedness is the one that is not general — σ̂² for the normal and the exponential rate estimator are both biased at every finite n.

items.stem: To find an MLE for a family whose support does not involve θ, arrange these steps.
items.explanation: Write the log-likelihood first, then differentiate and solve the likelihood equation, then confirm the stationary point is a maximum rather than a minimum or inflection, and only then apply invariance if the question asked for a function of θ. Checking the second-order condition is the step most often skipped and most often worth a mark.
items: B. Apply invariance if a function of θ was asked for
D. Verify the second-order condition for a maximum
